ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Multiverse Policy Learning with Robust Chi-Squared Regularization
PROPOSAL: Develop an extension to ORPO that instead of using a single reference policy, forms a probabilistic model of a distribution of possible policies. This multiverse model intrinsically accounts for variability in the true reward by considering all plausible reference policies that can coexist with the true reward given the proxy reward's correlation level, forming a class of correlated rewards. Then, during policy optimization, it penalizes the chi-squared divergence to all plausible policies, allowing the agent to converge to a policy that generalizes well even when the true correlation is uncertain or unknown. We will also formulate a tractable lower bound to enable optimization with standard RL tools.
CONTROLS: Compare to ORPO with a randomly chosen reference policy and to a baseline with no regularization.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will significantly improve robustness to variations in the proxy reward, but may suffer if the multiverse model is unable to capture all relevant plausible policies, leading to overly cautious exploration.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Learning Failure Modes of Weak Correlation
PROPOSAL: Design and train a pixel-perfect agent using a robust policy gradient estimator (e.g., TD3) on the highway merging subtask within the autonomous vehicle traffic control domain. We will then evaluate this agent on a "corruption" dataset, where we systematically perturb the strength and form of the correlation between proxy and true rewards. By correlating empirical failures of the agent to specific corruption patterns, we aim to identify failure modes of weak correlation that reveal underlying vulnerabilities to reward hacking. This study will either justify a lack of need for multiverse policy learning (if our results suggest that current agents are surprisingly robust to small perturbations in reward correlation) or yield crucial insights motivating its development (if previously unknown failure modes are discovered).
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard TD3 agent.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (assuming previously trained antibiotic policy can be leveraged)
PREDICTION: This study will uncover one or more previously unknown failure modes of weak correlation, which will guide the development of subsequent mitigation methods.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Robust Reward Shaping by Constrained Optimization
PROPOSAL:  Develop an approach that leverages constrained optimization to learn a robust reward function from the given proxy reward, the reference policy, and the assumed correlation level. We will formulate a constrained optimization problem where the true reward is constrained to be at least as strong as the proxy reward, up to a factor that depends on the correlation level. By solving this optimization problem, we can obtain a reward function that not only captures the proxy reward but also provides a lower bound on the true reward, thereby reducing the risk of reward hacking. This approach can be combined with multiverse policy learning to obtain even more robust policies.
CONTROLS: Compare to current state-of-the-art reward shaping methods.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will offer a promising solution for learning robust reward functions, but may suffer from the complexity of the constrained optimization problem, which could lead to slow convergence or intractability.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Graph-Based Model of the Multiverse
PROPOSAL:  Develop a graph-based model of the multiverse, where each node represents a possible policy and edges represent the similarity in behavior between policies. We will use a graph neural network to learn a representation of the multiverse that encodes the relationships between policies. This representation can be used to regularize the policy optimization objective, promoting a more diverse and robust set of policies. Additionally, the graph structure can be used to efficiently sample policies from the multiverse, allowing for more effective exploration.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the graph-based model on various metrics, including policy diversity and robustness.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will offer a scalable and efficient way to explore the multiverse, but may require careful tuning of the graph neural network architecture and hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Interpretability of Multiverse Policies via Network Disentanglement
PROPOSAL:  Develop a method for disentangling the policy optimization process and identifying the individual contributions of each policy to the overall behavior of the multiverse. By applying network disentanglement techniques to the graph-based model of the multiverse, we can identify clusters of policies that correspond to different modes of behavior. This will enable practitioners to understand which aspects of the policy are driving reward hacking and to identify potential vulnerabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare to current state-of-the-art methods for interpreting neural network policies.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will provide valuable insights into the behavior of multiverse policies, but may require careful tuning of the network disentanglement algorithms to ensure accurate results.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Online Multiverse Deployment for Safety-Critical Systems
PROPOSAL:  Develop an online deployment framework for safety-critical systems that uses the multiverse policy learning approach. The framework will continuously monitor the performance of the multiverse policies and adaptively update the policy to prevent reward hacking and ensure safe and reliable operation. Additionally, the framework will provide real-time monitoring and diagnosis of potential reward hacking incidents.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the online deployment framework on real-world safety-critical systems, such as autonomous vehicles.
COST: 6000 GPU-hours (assuming implementation of online deployment framework requires significant additional compute resources)
PREDICTION: This approach will offer a practical solution for deploying multiverse policy learning in safety-critical systems, but may require careful tuning of the online deployment framework to ensure robust and reliable operation.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Transferability of Multiverse Policies across Domains
PROPOSAL:  Investigate the transferability of multiverse policies across different domains, such as autonomous vehicle traffic control, pandemic response, and blood glucose control. We will evaluate the effectiveness of policies learned in one domain in the others and analyze the factors that contribute to transferability, including the similarity of the reward functions, the complexity of the environments, and the amount of training data.
CONTROLS: Compare to current state-of-the-art transfer learning methods.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study will provide valuable insights into the transferability of multiverse policies and shed light on the limitations of current approaches to transfer learning, but may require careful design of the experimental setup to ensure accurate results.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Synthesis of Multiverse Approaches with Human Expertise
PROPOSAL:  Investigate the integration of multiverse policy learning with human expertise, in particular with the help of domain experts (e.g. outcomes designers or model tormenters). We will explore how human feedback and domain knowledge can be incorporated into the multiverse policy learning framework to further improve the robustness and generalizability of learned policies. This may involve developing new methods for incorporating human feedback into the multiverse framework, or exploring how the multiverse framework can be used to improve the design of human-in-the-loop systems.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the integrated approach on various metrics, including policy robustness and human satisfaction.
COST: 5500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study will provide valuable insights into the potential of integrating human expertise with multiverse policy learning, but may require careful design of the human-in-the-loop setup to ensure accurate results.

This concludes the list of proposals.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Multiverse Policy Learning with Robust Chi-Squared Regularization
PROPOSAL: We learn a set of policies across a range of possible proxy rewards that are consistent with the assumed correlation constraint. Classifying each policy using true reward and its corresponding proxy reward, we select the policy with the highest correlation across the policy set. To do this, we augment the policy optimization objective with a robust form of chi-squared regularization, penalizing the difference between the policy's occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, under the most adversarial proxy among the set.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Learning using a single proxy reward and ORPO, Ablation: Learning using multiple proxies without robust regularization, Proposed baseline for ORPO: without the preference for the highest correlated policy.
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: Expected result: improving robustness to variations in proxy rewards, potential risk of overcompensating on the worst-case scenario and getting overly conservative policies and modeling computational cost that could slow down convergence, or underestimating constraints, so drawbacks kick in.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Unified Formulation of Weakly-Coupled Rewards as Stochastic Polytopes
PROPOSAL: We define a novel stochastic polytope model that captures the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint, and derive a tractable optimization objective that minimizes a weighted sum of the polynomial moments of the proxy reward, taking into account the uncertainty in the correlation level. The objective is parameterized by the correlation level and solution set used in our multiverse policy learning, providing a feasible and robust optimisation framework for handling varied possible reward functions.
CONTROLS: Baseline: ORPO with fixed correlation level and Occupancy as reference policy, Ablation: Using uniform weight instead of optimized polynomial moments.
COST: 9600
PREDICTION: Expected result: this unified formulation can effectively account for the worst-case scenario, but is likely to become intractable for high-degree polynomials, while handling fragmentation and the loss of meaningfulness due to highly correlated reward values from low best proxy correlations.

TITLE: Partially Observable Reference Policy (PORP) for Increased Extrapolation Safety
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a partially observable reference policy to guide learning and limit the exploration to the regions similar to the ones observed in reference policy's behavior. Specifically, we learn a compact, approximately sufficient statistic of the reference policy using a variational autoencoder, allowing the policy optimization to focus on the discovery of more similar policies. The result is potentially better extrapolation performance, especially in scenarios where the reference policy is only partially observable or interpreted in noisy manners.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Multiverse Policy Learning with Robust Chi-Squared Regularization
REVISION: We incorporate a hierarchical ensemble approach to improve the robustness of multiverse policy learning. Specifically, we train multiple base models on different subsets of the multi-rewards and then combine their predictions using a hierarchical ensemble method. This approach allows us to leverage the strengths of each individual model while reducing their individual weaknesses, leading to more robust and accurate policy learning outcomes.
CONTROLS: Baseline: non-ensemble version of our multiverse policy learning, Ablation: removing the hierarchical ensemble method and using a simple voting scheme.
COST: 18256
PREDICTION: Expected result: improve the robustness and accuracy of policy learning, while potentially reducing the computational cost of training and evaluation.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Robust Reward Transfer for Safe and Generalizable Policy Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to transfer policies learned on a source domain with a proxy reward to a target domain with a different proxy reward. Our approach uses a robust reward transformation to align the rewards across the two domains, allowing the policy to generalize better to the target domain. We then use our hierarchical ensemble approach from Proposal 1 to improve the robustness of the transferred policy.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Directly applying the policy learned on the source domain to the target domain without any transformation, Ablation: Removing the robust reward transformation.
COST: 24336
PREDICTION: Expected result: improve the safety and generalizability of policy learning, particularly when transferring policies between domains with different reward functions.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: robust reward relaxation
PROPOSAL: We experiment with the Proxy-agnostic Risk Bound (PARB) framework, which bounds the true reward loss of a policy optimized under an r-correlated proxy using the chi-squared divergence between the learned and reference policies' state-action occupancy measures. We vary the correlation level and explore different regularization strengths, and study its robustness to proxy reward deviations. 
CONTROLS: We compare against a set of baselines, including ORPO (Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization) under different correlation levels, and a standard PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) agent without regularization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a moderate improvement in true reward performance when the proxy reward has high correlation with the true reward, and the regularization strength is properly tuned, though the robustness could fail if the proxy reward deviates significantly from the true one.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: uncertainty-aware regularization
PROPOSAL: We propose a Bayesian version of the regularization term used in ORPO, incorporating prior knowledge over the possible true rewards as a Gaussian process, and use variational inference to leverage the observed data and approximate the posterior over the latent variables. This approach allows us to penalize the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure based on our uncertainty about the true reward, and derive a probabilistic interpretation of the regularization term.
CONTROLS: We compare against the non-Bayesian version of the regularization term used in ORPO, and a set of baselines where the regularization term is not used.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a improved robustness to variations in the proxy reward, especially when there is a clear mismatch between the proxy and true rewards, and an increased interpretability of the learned policy, as the uncertainty estimates can be used to diagnose policy weaknesses in novel situations.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: robust reward relaxation
PROPOSAL: We extend the Proxy-agnostic Risk Bound (PARB) framework to incorporate uncertainty over the proxy reward itself, drawn from a Dirichlet process mixture model. This Bayesian version of PARB allows us to model the probability distribution over all possible proxy rewards consistent with the assumed correlation level, and obtain a probabilistic upper bound on the true reward loss. We then use variational inference to approximate the posterior over the proxy rewards, and adapt the regularization strength and chi-squared divergence term accordingly.
CONTROLS: We compare against the non-Bayesian version of PARB used in turn 1, and a set of baselines where the Bayesian version is used but the chi-squared divergence term is not regularized.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in true reward performance, especially when the proxy reward has low correlation with the true reward, but also a higher computational cost due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: exploration prioritization
PROPOSAL: We modify the greedy optimization procedure used in PARB and ORPO to prioritize exploratory actions that have the highest expected uncertainty reduction under the learned policy, using an upper confidence bound (UCB) strategy. This allows the agent to actively seek out state-action pairs where the correlation constraint is ambiguous, and gather more information about the true reward in these regions.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard greedy optimization procedure used in PARB and ORPO, and a set of baselines where exploration is not prioritized.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect an improved balance between exploitation and exploration, and a reduced risk of reward hacking, as the agent actively seeks out areas where more information is needed.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: uncertainty-aware regularization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of a hierarchical prior model over the true reward, which allows us to exploit partial knowledge about the reward structure in the form of a coarse-grained functional form. We use a Gaussian process to represent the reward function, with a hierarchy of kernel functions that encode the prior knowledge about the reward structure. This enables the agent to identify the most informative features of the reward, and adapt the regularization term accordingly.
CONTROLS: We compare against a set of baselines where the hierarchical prior model is not used, and the regularization term is based on a simple mean-squared error criterion.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect an improvement in the ability to exploit partial knowledge about the reward structure, and a more accurate identification of policy vulnerabilities to reward hacking, as the agent utilizes the hierarchy of kernel functions to encode the prior knowledge.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: interpretable policy optimization
PROPOSAL: We develop a proxy-agnostic policy optimization framework that yields interpretable policies by encoding the learned policy as a linear combination of a set of underlying, reward-linked features. We use a sparse regression formulation to identify the most relevant features, which are then used to regularize the policy optimization procedure. This approach enables us to diagnose policy weaknesses and identify which aspects of the reward are being exploited by the agent.
CONTROLS: We compare against a set of baselines where the policy is not encoded as a linear combination of features, and the interpretation is not provided.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in the interpretability of the learned policies, and a better understanding of which features of the reward are being exploited by the agent, though a potential trade-off in policy performance may occur.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: robust reward relaxation
PROPOSAL: We modify the Proxy-agnostic Risk Bound (PARB) framework to incorporate a penalty term that promotes policies with a simpler geometry, as measured by the covering number of the policy's state-action space. This regularization term encourages the agent to avoid over-complex policies that are more susceptible to reward hacking.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard PARB framework without the geometric regularization term, and a set of baselines where the regularization term is based on a simple mean-squared error criterion.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a reduction in the risk of reward hacking, especially for high-dimensional state-action spaces, as the agent is encouraged to learn simpler policies that are less prone to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: multi-task reward learning
PROPOSAL: We extend the PARB framework to support multi-task reward learning by jointly optimizing multiple reward functions that capture different aspects of the true reward. This allows us to transfer knowledge between tasks and adapt the policy to novel reward functions that are consistent with the assumed correlation constraint.
CONTROLS: We compare against a set of baselines where each task is optimized separately, and a set of baselines where the tasks are optimized using a shared policy but separate reward functions.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect an improvement in the ability to adapt to novel reward functions, and a faster learning rate for new tasks, as the agent leverages the shared knowledge acquired during previous tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: multi-task reward learning
PROPOSAL: We modify the multi-task reward learning framework to incorporate an ensemble approach, where multiple policies are learned in parallel, each specialized to a different aspect of the true reward. We use a multi-task actor-critic algorithm to learn the ensemble of policies, and select the final policy using a subset of the tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard multi-task reward learning framework without the ensemble approach, and a set of baselines where each policy is learned separately.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect an improved robustness to variations in the true reward, and a better handling of noisy and uncertain rewards, as the ensemble of policies provides a more diverse set of solutions to the reward hacking problem.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: transferable risk bounds
PROPOSAL: We develop a theory of transferable risk bounds, which allows us to translate the risk bounds obtained in one task or environment to a different task or environment. We show that this can be achieved by using a representation-based approach, where the risk bounds are expressed in terms of the learned representations or features of the task.
CONTROLS: We compare against a set of baselines where the risk bounds are not transferred, and a set of baselines where a separate set of risk bounds is learned for each task.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in the ability to transfer knowledge and risk bounds across different tasks and environments, and a more efficient learning process, as the agent can leverage the existing knowledge and risk bounds to adapt to new situations.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Multiverse Policy Learning with Robust Chi-Squared Regularization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new policy optimization algorithm, "Multiverse Policy Learning" (MPL), that extends ORPO to learn a policy robust to variations in proxy rewards. MPL generates a set of policies, each optimized with a chi-squared regularization term, but with a strength dependent on the proxy reward's correlation level, drawn from a Bayesian prior distribution. The algorithm maximizes a lower-bounded objective function that takes into account the proxy-true reward correlation and the policy's robustness properties.
CONTROLS: Compare MPL to ORPO and the baseline SArchive (State-Regularized Actor-Critic) on various synthetic datasets with r-correlated proxy rewards, including preference-based and visual datasets like the Proc_gen dataset and Program-Animated Episode corpus, which can model pandemic response (lockdown policy) or blood glucose control scenarios.
COST: 576
PREDICTION: MPL should outperform ORPO, with sample complexity and robustness benefits, possibly failing in fine-tuning drawbacks due to increased hyperparameter space. More proceess recovered with trials though, and seem sharp improvement.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Unified Formulation of Weakly-Correlated Rewards as Stochastic Polytopes
PROPOSAL: Theoretically formalize the class of proxy rewards consistent with a given correlation level r and the reference policy's occupancy measure. Show that such rewards can be represented as the intersection of stochastic polytopes, where each polytope corresponds to one state-action pair, parametrized by r. Develop a tractable algorithm to compute this representation, which can guide the design of future approaches to robust RL under weak correlations. 
CONTROLS: Compare the number of constraints required for the proposed parametrization to existing methods, as well as its efficiency in representing the complexity of the reward space for varying r.
COST: 192
PREDICTION: The proposal reveals the fundamental geometric structure of weakly-correlated rewards, potentially identifying a "regime of opportunity" for discovering efficient methods. Future analyses might struggle with wider correlations.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Multiverse Policy Learning with Robust Chi-Squared Regularization Improved by Polytopes-based Prior

TITLE: Reverse Diffusion Inversion via Latent Space Transport
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to solving inverse problems by leveraging the recently developed transport map gradient sampler, which efficiently samples from the target distribution by leveraging a pre-computed transport map. We will use this sampler within the context of a pretrained diffusion model to sample from the posterior p(x|y). To this end, we will define a new transport map that maps from the intermediate diffused states of the reverse diffusion process to the learned manifold of the denoiser, with the output of this map serving as input to the conditional denoiser. By feeding the pre-computed transport map as a guidance signal to the intermediate states of the reverse diffusion process, we can ensure that these states stay on the learned manifold while still allowing us to explore different modes of the posterior.
CONTROLS: The baseline methods will include a standard deterministic MAP method that optimizes the input noise of the diffusion model, and an iterative guidance GAN-based method. We will also test ablated versions of our approach that either use a randomly initialized transport map, or remove the use of the transport map entirely.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: I expect our method to significantly outperform the baseline methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness to noise. Failure may occur when the learned manifold of the denoiser is poorly aligned with the true data manifold, or when there is significant mode collapse in the posterior.

We will initialize the width-adaptive network with a small width and gradually increase it as the hierarchical sampling proceeds, allowing the network to refine its estimates of the posterior modes. This allows us to better capture the multimodality of the posterior and to avoid getting stuck in local minima.

This will be achieved by using a noise-conditional denoiser, which takes both the noisy measurement and an estimate of the noise distribution as input. We will train the noise-conditional denoiser jointly with the inverse problem solver, allowing the denoiser to learn the optimal noise model online. This will enable our approach to handle unknown or non-Gaussian noise distributions without requiring task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

TITLE: Hierarchical Sampling for Inverse Problems with Unknown Measurement Noise
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of unknown measurement noise, we propose a hierarchical sampling approach that uses a two-stage process. This adaptation allows us to robustly sample the posterior even when the measurement noise level is unknown, thereby improving the solver's robustness to noise variability.
CONTROLS: We will compare this approach to state-of-the-art deterministic MAP solvers like DMPlug and existing stochastic MAP solvers that rely on heuristically set noise levels.

ACTION: REVISE (2)
TITLE: fine-tuning high-capacity conditional generators with biased reward functions
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of biased reward functions to guide the fine-tuning of pre-trained high-capacity conditional generators towards increased diversity. Specifically, reward functions will be designed to maximize the mutual information between generated and real image distributions, while penalizing over-specialization. Use the previously established zero-shot diversity loss estimator to quantify the generated diversity.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed biased reward functions against standard rewards (e.g., VGG-based perceptual loss, adversarial loss) and ablate the proposed diversity regularization term. Also control for different fine-tuning schedules and architectures (e.g., VAEs, autoencoders).
COST: 128 GPU-hours (predicted).
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning with biased rewards should lead to improved diversity in generated images, but may compromise on quality. The model may over-specialize or converge to a suboptimal solution, highlighting the need for careful tuning of the reward function and regularization strength.

ACTION: ADD (3)
TITLE: multi-exemplar contextualized guidance for improved diversity
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-exemplar approach to contextualized guidance for conditional image generators, where the generator is conditioned on a set of real exemplar images. This is in contrast to prior work that used only a single exemplar image. Investigate the impact of increasing the number of exemplars on generated diversity and quality using both biased reward functions and the nonparametric diversity loss estimator.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed multi-exemplar approach against a single-exemplar baseline (c-VSG) and a variety of other exemplar-based guidance methods.
COST: 64 GPU-hours (predicted).
PREDICTION: The multi-exemplar approach should lead to improved diversity in generated images, but may compromise on quality due to increased conditioning complexity. The benefits of increased exemplars will depend on the specific model architecture, reward function, and diversity regularization strength used.

ACTION: ADD (4)
TITLE: collective diversity regularization via conditional auxiliary losses
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel loss regularization technique that encourages the generator to produce diverse outputs by conditioning on the collective diversity of the entire generated batch, rather than individual samples. This is achieved by introducing a conditional auxiliary loss that measures the diversity of the generated batch with respect to the training data. Compare the effectiveness of this approach against standard diversity regularization techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous fine-tuning approach and the multi-exemplar contextualized guidance method, as well as standard diversity regularization baselines (e.g., min-max entropy loss, mixture loss).
COST: 80 GPU-hours (predicted).
PREDICTION: The collective diversity regularization approach should lead to improved diversity in generated images, as it encourages the model to produce a diverse set of outputs that collectively span the training data space. However, it may also compromise on quality due to increased computational complexity.

ACTION: ADD (5)
TITLE: selecting exemplars for contextualized guidance using active learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of active learning to select a diverse and informative set of exemplar images for contextualized guidance. This involves iteratively querying the generator with newly generated images and selecting the most informative ones to add to the exemplar set. Compare the effectiveness of this approach against random sampling and other active learning strategies.
CONTROLS: Compare against the multi-exemplar contextualized guidance method and ablate the active learning component by using randomly selected exemplars.
COST: 48 GPU-hours (predicted).
PREDICTION: The active learning approach should lead to improved diversity and quality of generated images, as it selectively chooses exemplars that are most informative for the generator. However, it may also increase computational complexity due to the iterative selection process.

ACTION: ADD (6)

PROPOSAL: Develop a method for reducing geographic bias in conditional image generators by using contextualized guidance with exemplars from diverse world regions. Investigate the impact of this approach on reducing bias and improving diversity of generated images.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline generator trained on a globally diverse dataset and ablate the contextualized guidance component.
COST: 32 GPU-hours (predicted).
PREDICTION: The contextualized guidance approach should lead to reduced geographic bias in generated images and improved diversity, as it selectively adjusts the generator's output to align with exemplars from diverse world regions. However, it may also introduce new biases if the exemplars are not carefully selected.

For the text retriever, we will use the Wikipedia dataset as a training set and the MS MARCO passage ranking dataset as a testing set. For visual document retrieval, we will use the visual set of the CXC dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Back-Propagation through Tokenizer Decoding
PROPOSAL: We modify the Di[M]O distillation procedure to keep track of the gradients flowing through the pre-trained tokenizer decoder. We pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation using the " Straight Through Estimator" (STE) and augment the teacher's loss with the cross-entropy term between the decoder's outputs and the true image pixels. This allows gradients to flow back to the teacher and, by extension, to the student, and aligns the teacher with the downstream reward model's preferred image characteristics.
CONTROLS: We compare with the original Di[M]O procedure and a variant that uses the STE but without the augmenting cross-entropy loss.
COST: 9,432
PREDICTION: Backpropagating gradients through the tokenizer decoder should help align the teacher with the downstream objectives, especially in text-to-image generation where the tokenizer decoder has a significant impact on the generated image. However, it might struggle to fully correct the alignment errors inherited from the teacher, and the STE might introduce instability or bias in the gradients.

The STE is a simple and effective method to bypass the non-differentiable sampler, but it remains to be seen whether it is sufficient to handle the complex relationship between the discrete tokens and the image pixels.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: We modify the Di[M]O distillation procedure to directly incorporate the downstream reward model's output into the student's loss function. This allows the student to learn from the reward model's preferences and correct the errors inherited from the teacher.

PROPOSAL: Design a general framework, known as Adaptive Cropping (AC), that adaptively selects and crops the most relevant regions of interest for a given VQA task without requiring task-specific fine-tuning or multiple forward passes. CONTROLS: Evaluate AC on various VQA benchmarks and compare its performance to recent VQA state-of-the-art models that employ hierarchical search and cropping methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Regional Proposal Generation for Visual Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We introduce a non-local attention-based generator for regional proposals, using a Vision Transformer (ViT) that leverages global information from the image to focus on regions relevant to the question. This approach, named QKG (Query-and-Keyword-Generator), is guided by a query that represents the question and a keyword that captures the visual context. QKG allows us to efficiently generate a small set of region proposals by aggregating local and global information in a self-attention mechanism. We further enhance QKG with a learned image feature subsetter that helps to reduce redundant region proposals by selecting the most informative features.
CONTROLS: We compare QKG with LightCrop's visual search strategy from proposal 1 and baseline methods SEAL and DC².
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: QKG improves accuracy on fine-grained VQA tasks compared to LightCrop, but may suffer from decreased efficiency when generating region proposals.

PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical, soft-Regional - consensus model inspired by graph networks to guide regional crop for grounding in Visual Question Answering tasks. Our Hierarchical Soft Regional Consensus (HSRC) module is a hierarchical classifier that labels each region as relevant or irrelevant to the question, aggregating information from higher-level abstract representations to fine-grained location features. We combine the predictions of the HSRC module with the original image to obtain a weighted soft-Label vector that seamlessly integrates global and local information for more accurate answer prediction. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mutual-Benefit Deep Fusion of Image and Question Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel deep fusion approach that aligns and integrates both image and question embeddings in a shared space to enhance the effectiveness of visual question answering models. This approach, Mutual-Benefit Embeddings (MBE), considers the contextual semantics of the image and the question through a computationally efficient framework, which benefits from a unified vision-linguistic embedding space. By synergistically fusing both visual and linguistic information, MBE facilitates better comprehension and understanding of multimodal data, ensuring the effective identification of query-relevant image regions. To improve existing MLLM models, MBE can serve as a complement to strategies like LightCrop and QKG.
CONTROLS: Compare MBE's fusion scheme with concatenation-based methods and visualize the benefits of MBE-fused embeddings through t-SNE or PCA.
COST: 5400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MBE significantly improves the performance of existing MLLMs on fine-grained VQA tasks by learning more meaningful and contextually aligned image and question embeddings, while its efficiency may vary depending on the specific implementation and complexity of the task.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised: Efficient Regional Proposal Generation for Visual Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We refine the non-local attention-based generator for regional proposals, QKG, by incorporating a more efficient and robust feature aggregation mechanism. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Graph Attention for Visual Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel multi-modal graph attention network, MMGAN, to enhance the fusion of visual and textual information in VQA. MMGAN represents the image and text as nodes in a graph and leverages attention mechanisms to capture the complex relationships between them. By iteratively refining the attention weights, MMGAN effectively adapts to the dynamic nature of the VQA task, allowing for more efficient and accurate fusion of the input modalities. Additionally, we propose a novel modal-aware residual learning mechanism to mitigate the potential drift in attention weights caused by the distinct characteristics of the visual and textual modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare MMGAN with existing state-of-the-art VQA methods, including LightCrop, QKG, and HSRC.
COST: 10800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MMGAN demonstrates improved accuracy and robustness on fine-grained VQA tasks, leveraging the power of graph attention and modal-aware residual learning to capture complex relationships between visual and textual information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Refining Visual Search for Efficient Visual Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a self-supervised visual co-training (SSVCT) strategy to localize image regions relevant to the question without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules can outperform the ViCrop and other visual cropping methods.
We modify the existing pre-training objective for the MLLM by having it predict a weighted heatmap for each input image, where the weights come from the ground-truth captions or other auxiliary sources. On top of the standard pre-training objective, we add a contrastive loss that encourages the weighted heatmap to match the precise region of interest that is represented by one of the auxiliary sources. During inference, we use this pre-trained MLLM to generate a weighted heatmap that highlights the regions relevant to the question. We discard areas with low weights and pass the rest to the global-view or global-local-view MLLM.
CONTROLS: Compare our method with state-of-the-art visual cropping methods on two benchmark datasets for visual question answering, e.g., the Stanford Cars Dataset and the Visual Genome Dataset, using the apparatus of ViCrop and evaluating its accuracy and efficiency.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our method to perform on par with ViCrop while being more computationally efficient, thanks to not requiring explicit object bounding box predictions or dependencies on query-key attention weights and answer gradients.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Impact of Region of Interest Guidance on Global-View MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether explicitly guiding the vision encoder of a global-view MLLM towards the region of interest predicted by our SSVCT strategy in 1 (Refining Visual Search for Efficient Visual Question Answering) can improve its performance on fine-grained visual questions, while keeping inference cost low.
We design an attention-scaled ROI guide for the vision encoder by re-weighting the input tokens based on the highest weighted heatmap values from our SSVCT strategy. To preserve computational efficiency, we ensure the guided tokens fit within the encoder's receptive field.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effects of different guided ROI sizes (e.g., 32x32, 80x80, 160x160) on the fine-grained VQA task on the Stanford Cars Dataset and evaluate the impact of ROI guidance on the model's performance relative to the baseline global-view MLLM.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With proper selection of the ROI size, we expect our approach to facilitate more efficient learning of high-resolution visual features from the region of interest, thereby leading to improved performance on fine-grained VQA tasks while reducing the number of unnecessary visual tokens processed during inference.

TITLE: contrastive learning from neuropixels time series
PROPOSAL: We will implement a contrastive learning framework for jointly learning neuron-representations from Neuropixels recordings and identity labels. This will involve training a neural network to learn a latent representation that maximizes the agreement between representations of labeled neuron activity across batches and minimizes the agreement between representations of unlabeled activity and labeled activity from different neurons. We will train the network on 10k Neuropixels recordings from mice brain regions, with relatively sparse identity labels (one class per 100 neurons on average).
CONTROLS: Baseline models include Noise-contrastive estimation (NCE) for unsupervised feature learning, and simple supervised learning on waveform shape and frequency features.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results include improved preliminary classification accuracy and distance metrics between clusters of neurons, assuming no overfitting and well-tuned hyperparameters. Possible failure scenarios involve mismatched data distributions due to measurement noise and artifacts.

PROPOSAL: We propose a decision-level fusion framework that uses knowledge distillation to convey side information from the dominant modality to the weak one, helping it improve its performance without adopting its errors. The framework will employ a teacher-student architecture, where the dominant modality is the teacher and the weak modality is the student. The teacher model produces a fused prediction and a sharpened distillation criterion to guide the student. In each iteration, the student model receives a combination of the true labels and the distillation criterion as targets to optimize, thus leveraging the weak modality's own prediction and the distilled information to refine its performance.
CONTROLS: Vanilla late fusion with identical weights, uncertainty-based robust late fusion using aleatoric uncertainty.

PREDICTION: The experimental results show a significant improvement in both accuracy and robustness of the fused prediction when using distilled side information, with a closer but non-overlapping gap in performance between the strong and weak modalities. While this setup achieves robustness, we anticipate that its benefits might dwindle in settings with extreme imbalance, where the weak modality is vastly outperformed, and the teacher's confidence is influential.

TITLE: REVISED 2. Robust Period Fusion with Dynamic Gaussian Process for Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL:  We combine a robust dynamic periodic modeling module built on Gaussian processes with multi-tasking learning to model periodic variability in univariate time series. The model learns to capture both the short-term and long-term patterns in the data, enabling it to detect subtle anomalies and noise. To further improve the performance of the model, we use a transfer learning strategy, pre-training the model on a large dataset of univariate time series and fine-tuning it on the target dataset.

PREDICTION:  We expect our approach to outperform the baselines by 10-15% in terms of anomaly detection accuracy, while also improving the robustness and adaptability of the model.

TITLE: Ensemble Method for Anomaly Detection in Univariate Time Series Data
PROPOSAL: We propose an ensemble method that combines the strengths of multiple anomaly detection models for univariate time series data. The ensemble method consists of three components: a local autoregression-based model, a dynamic Gaussian process-based model, and a novel kernel-based model. Each component is trained on the same dataset, and the final anomaly scores are obtained by voting across the three components. The kernel-based model is designed to capture long-term patterns and trends in the data, while the local autoregression model captures short-term fluctuations. The dynamic Gaussian process model is used to capture periodic patterns and variability.

CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach against individual models (proposals 1 and 2) and against a state-of-the-art ensemble method ( Bagging).

COST: 18000
PREDICTION:  We expect our ensemble method to outperform individual models by 5-10% and the Bagging method by 2-5% in terms of anomaly detection accuracy.

TITLE: Temporal Attention Mechanism for Anomaly Detection in Univariate Time Series
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel Temporal Attention Mechanism (TAM) that captures the temporal dependencies and patterns in univariate time series data. The TAM uses a weighted sum of past observations to compute the current anomaly score, where the weights are learned through a self-attention mechanism. This allows the model to focus on the most relevant past observations when computing the current anomaly score. We also use a novel clustering-based anomaly score aggregation method to effectively combine the anomaly scores from multiple TAM modules.

CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach against individual models (proposals 1-3) and against a state-of-the-art attention-based anomaly detection method.

COST: 20000
PREDICTION:  We expect our TAM method to outperform individual models by 5-10% and the state-of-the-art attention-based method by 2-5% in terms of anomaly detection accuracy.

TITLE: Dynamic Local Autoregression (DLAR) for Univariate Time Series
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel unsupervised anomaly detector for UTS based on a dynamic local autoregression (DLAR) model, which captures both temporal dependencies and fluctuating local trends. DLAR will generate a set of local autoregressive models, each conditioned on a specific time window, to adapt to the changing first-order stochastic properties of the series. For each window of consecutive data points, the model will learn to predict the next observation based on its immediate neighbors.
CONTROLS: Compare DLAR with two popular reconstruction-based methods, one-step-ahead moving average (MA) and local piecewise aggregate approximation (LPAQ), and with a baseline prediction model such as the popular Prophet algorithm.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: DLAR outperforms the baselines in detecting small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies, and its dynamic local modeling component helps to handle evolving periodic patterns, but it struggles with modeling complex long-term dependencies and is affected by the noise level.

PROPOSAL: Develop a novel unsupervised method for modeling evolving periodic patterns in UTS, called Periodicity Binning Estimation (PBE). PBE leverages a learned frequency binning approach, where learned frequency components from successive time windows are adaptively compensated to capture changing periodic periods, and estimates the evolving periodic behavior through periodic transformations that are applied to each local trend, obtained from the DLAR model introduced in Experiment 1.
CONTROLS: Compare PBE with traditional methods for periodicity estimation, such as the Lomb-Scargle periodogram and Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), in terms of their ability to detect slope variations and frequency adjustments.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: PBE outperforms the baselines in estimating evolving periodic patterns and handles noise robustly, but requires careful tuning of the learned frequency binning parameters, and a higher regime-specific data signal is necessary to reduce bias.

PROPOSAL: Propose a novel neural architecture called Temporal Attention for Univariate (TAU) anomaly detection, which incorporates a temporal attention mechanism into a univariate sequence model. TAU learns to selectively focus on the most relevant contiguous parts of the time series history when determining whether a current data point is anomalous. The temporal attention mechanism helps to alleviate the issue of neglecting long-term context and adaptation to UTS specific requirements, while the attention truly cares about relevance, not length, when it is applied.

PROPOSAL: 
We will start by empirically investigating inter-modal catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs, focusing on two tasks: visual question answering (VQA) and text-to-image generation. We'll train a UMGM on a large-scale dataset (e.g., VQA-V2 and COCO) and then fine-tune it on subsequent tasks in a sequence, tracking performance on both VQA and text-to-image generation. This will be our baseline experiment to establish whether UMGMs suffer from inter-modal forgetting.

- Baseline 1: UMGM trained from scratch on each task.
- Baseline 2: UMGM pre-trained on a large-scale dataset and fine-tuned on subsequent tasks, but without instruction tuning.

COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a significant drop in performance on the pre-trained modality when fine-tuning the model on subsequent tasks in a sequence, indicating inter-modal catastrophic forgetting. However, the extent of forgetting may vary across tasks and models.

 PROPOSAL: We derive new theory to bound the error of representing 3D Gaussian anisotropic scale and rotation with a low-resolution neural field, assuming the gauge invariance of neural networks and assuming the 3D Gaussians can be partitioned into a collection of orthonormal basis Gaussians. Using this result, we propose and prove the convergence of a new optimization algorithm that alternatively refines the neural field's representation of Gaussian properties and reconstructs the 3D Gaussians using the low-resolution field. This approach can provably recover high-frequency details that grid-based neural fields tend to miss.
 CONTROLS: Compare against current grid-based neural field methods, and also against a baseline where we use the orthogonal basis approximations directly without neural field refinement.

By inserting GPLs between standard neural field layers, we can dynamically adjust the resolution of the Gaussian representation to suit the local needs of the scene, effectively capturing high-frequency details in regions of rapid change while maintaining compactness elsewhere. We train GPLs to jointly optimize the partitioning and the neural field representation, incorporating the orthogonality constraints and the desired precision of the Gaussians.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of information-theoretic concepts, specifically entropy control, to regulate the amount of detail in the generated images and adapt it to the available bitrate. PROPOSAL: Investigate the problem of partial dictionary recovery, where the goal is to recover a subset of the latent variables rather than the entire dictionary. This is a common scenario in many real-world applications, where only a small subset of the relevant features is of interest. Develop a novel method that leverages the inductive biases for recovery (Proposal 2) and transfer learning (Proposal 4) to.enable partial dictionary recovery.
CONTROLS: Compare the recovery performance to a baseline method that uses a standard dictionary learning algorithm, as well as to a method that uses a combination of the inductive biases for recovery and temporal hierarchy (Proposal 3).
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours on a synthetic dataset with a subset of the latent variables.
PREDICTION: We anticipate finding that our method can recover the relevant subset of latent variables more effectively than the baseline methods, especially when the subset is small and the remaining variables are noisy or irrelevant.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: nonparametric dictionary learning without strong assumptions
PROPOSAL: Refine the theoretical guarantee for the recovery of a latent generative process in the general nonparametric setting, exploring whether it is possible to achieve a more robust and generalizable guarantee by incorporating the inductive biases for recovery (Proposal 2) and transfer learning (Proposal 4). Specifically, consider the regime where the generating function is smooth and injective but otherwise unknown, and investigate whether the addition of these biases can ensure recovery up to a permutation for any smooth and injective generating function.
CONTROLS: Compare the new theoretical guarantee to existing methods that rely on parametric assumptions or auxiliary information, as well as to the previous guarantee that assumed a fixed bias.
COST: Estimated 10 GPU-hours on a theoretical analysis of the new guarantee.
PREDICTION: We anticipate finding that incorporating the inductive biases for recovery and transfer learning strengthens the theoretical guarantee, making it more robust and generalizable to various generative processes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: application to language models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the proposed methods for dictionary recovery on a real-world task: interpreting the hidden representations of a pre-trained language model. Specifically, use the inductive biases for recovery (Proposal 2), transfer learning (Proposal 4), and partial dictionary recovery (Proposal 5) to analyze the latent space of a state-of-the-art language model and identify meaningful clusters, tags, or sub-dimensions that correspond to specific linguistic or semantic concepts.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to standard baselines, such as principal component analysis (PCA) or k-means clustering, and explore the interpretability of the recovered dictionary.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours on a large pre-trained language model.
PREDICTION: We anticipate finding that the proposed methods can uncover meaningful and interpretable patterns in the latent space of the language model, providing insights into the representation of linguistic and semantic concepts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating robustness to domain shifts
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of the proposed dictionary recovery methods to domain shifts, where the distribution of the data changes between the training and testing sets. Specifically, evaluate the transferability of the recovered dictionaries across different datasets, domains, or languages, and analyze how the inductive biases for recovery (Proposal 2) and transfer learning (Proposal 4) impact the robustness of the recovered dictionaries.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the proposed methods to standard baselines, such as dictionaries learned on a single domain or without transfer learning.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours on a set of domain-shifted datasets.
PREDICTION: We anticipate finding that the proposed methods can recover dictionaries that are robust to domain shifts, especially when combined with the transfer learning and inductive biases. However, we may also identify challenges and limitations, such as overfitting or loss of interpretability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: minimal dictionary recovery
PROPOSAL: Investigate the minimum number of samples required for efficient dictionary recovery in the general nonparametric setting. Specifically, analyze the trade-off between the number of samples and the recovery performance of the proposed methods, and identify the minimal requirements for achieving reliable and robust dictionary recovery.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed methods under various sample sizes, and evaluate the impact of sample size on the interpretability and robustness of the recovered dictionaries.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours on a set of datasets with varying sample sizes.
PREDICTION: We anticipate finding that the proposed methods can recover dictionaries efficiently even with a small number of samples, but may need to adapt or refine the choice of inductive biases to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structural Assumptions for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of structural assumptions on identifiability in nonlinear dictionary learning. Specifically, we will explore whether incorporating sparsity, smoothness, or injectivity into the generative process can guarantee recovery of latent variables under minimal assumptions. We will derive bounds on the number of required measurements and analyze the effect of noise on estimation accuracy.
CONTROLS: Linear dictionary learning (baseline), semi-supervised dictionary learning (ablation), and no structural assumptions (ablation)
COST: 100
PREDICTION: Under sufficient sparsity or smoothness conditions, we expect to recover a large number of latent variables with high precision, but may fail when assuming injectivity, as this condition can be overly restrictive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neural Network-Based Modeling of the Generative Process
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based framework for modeling the non-linear generative process in dictionary learning. Specifically, we will train a neural network to approximate the mapping from latent variables to observations. We will evaluate its ability to recover latent variables without imposing strong parametric constraints on the generative process.
CONTROLS: Linear dictionary learning (baseline), structural assumptions for nonlinear dictionary learning (ablation of proposal 1), and a randomly initialized neural network (ablation)
COST: 500
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to improve recovery accuracy, but may overfit to the training data, especially when the network is complex or the number of training samples is limited.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Neural Network-Based Modeling of the Generative Process
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to incorporate recent advances in sparse and regularized neural networks, such as sparse-net or split-net, to promote sparsity and smoothness in the generative process. This may help improve recovery accuracy and provide a more interpretable model. We will also investigate the effect of these regularizations on the learned neural network's representation capacity.
CONTROLS: Original neural network-based framework (ablation), linear dictionary learning (baseline), and the modified sparse neural network-based framework
COST: 400
PREDICTION: The sparse neural network-based framework is likely to improve recovery accuracy and provide a more interpretable model, but may introduce additional computational costs due to the sparsity constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bayesian Model Comparison for Identifiability
PROPOSAL: Develop a Bayesian framework for comparing competing models of the generative process in dictionary learning. We will use Bayesian model selection and model averaging techniques to evaluate the evidence for different models and quantify the uncertainty associated with model estimates. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the identifiability of latent variables under different modeling assumptions.
CONTROLS: Linear dictionary learning (baseline), neural network-based modeling of the generative process (ablation), and a non-informative prior (ablation)
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The Bayesian framework is likely to provide a more nuanced understanding of model identifiability, but may require computationally expensive inference procedures and may struggle with model overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of transfer learning for nonlinear dictionary learning, where a pre-trained model is adapted to a new task or domain. CONTROLS: Linear dictionary learning (baseline), neural network-based modeling of the generative process (ablation), and a pre-trained neural network (transfer learning)
COST: 200
PREDICTION: Transfer learning is likely to improve recovery accuracy, especially when the pre-trained model is similar to the target task, but may also introduce domain mismatch and overfitting issues if not handled carefully.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis with Frozen Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of frozen multimodal large language models for zero-shot video anomaly analysis by leveraging temporal, spatial, and textual cues captured within the model's pre-trained weights. Specifically, test the effectiveness of using coarse-grained temporal annotations (start time, end time, and anomaly type) in conjunction with fine-tuned vision-language prompt templates to generate textual explanations for video anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare performance with a zero-shot baseline that uses a frozen vision-language model to generate frame-wise anomaly scores without textual explanations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (exploring 5 different prompt templates and 3 different vision-language models).
PREDICTION: The proposed approach will achieve better performance than the baseline in detecting and explaining video anomalies, with robustness across domains and anomaly types, but may struggle with anomalies that require fine-grained spatial information or complex explanations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Explanations for Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to generate adversarial explanations for the zero-shot video anomaly analysis model proposed in the previous experiment. This will involve using a text generator to craft adversarial prompts that confuse the model and reduce its performance. Evaluate the effectiveness of the adversarial explanations by assessing the model's robustness to these attacks.
CONTROLS: Compare robustness to a model trained with adversarial training and a model without any adversarial training.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (exploring 5 different attack methods and 2 different models).
PREDICTION: The proposed approach will successfully generate adversarial explanations that reduce the model's performance, and the model trained with adversarial training will exhibit better robustness to these attacks. However, the robustness gains may come at the cost of reduced accuracy on clean data.

PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive method that learns to weigh pseudo-labels using attention mechanisms, which dynamically allocate weights based on the relevance of each pseudo-label to the target task. This approach allows the model to selectively focus on reliable pseudo-labels while down-weighting uncertain or noisy ones, which can lead to improved segmentation performance, especially when the pseudo-labels are noisy or class-ambiguous.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method against standard self-training and consistency regularization methods, as well as against a baseline that applies uniform weighting to pseudo-labels.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance compared to standard pseudo-label learning methods, especially in cases where the pseudo-labels are noisy and there is a high degree of class ambiguity. However, we also expect to see potential challenges in optimizing the attention mechanisms, which could lead to increased computational complexity.

This proposal addresses a different aspect of the noisy pseudo-label problem, focusing on the adaptive weighting of pseudo-labels rather than encoding or entropy minimization. It is complementary to the previous proposals and can be combined with them for further improvement.

This can potentially improve the robustness of pseudo-labels to noise and class ambiguity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-Step Generative Model with Improved Stability
PROPOSAL: Train a consistency model variant, PCM (Progressive Contrastive Mining), but incorporate a feedback loop which adapts the diffusion schedule at each step, allowing the model to adjust the progress based on the output quality from the previous steps. Specifically, after step 't', the model computes a "quality metric" for current image quality, and uses it to adjust the learning rate, strength of noise addition, or the step size for noise reduction in the subsequent step.
CONTROLS: PCM model with static diffusion schedule (no feedback loop), GLIDE model (baseline for sampling in few steps)
COST: Estimated 10k GPU-hours using a 4-A100 GPU cluster
PREDICTION: We expect the adapted schedule will improve sampling quality, especially at lower NFEs (e.g., fewer than 8), but may lead to overfitting if not implemented carefully, as it introduces an additional learning mechanism that may interact with the existing dynamics in an unpredictable manner.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Introduce an alternative loss function for training PCM with the feedback loop, replacing the original mean squared error with a perceptual loss (e.g., VGG loss) and a consistency loss. COST: Estimated 2k GPU-hours using the same 4-A100 GPU cluster
PREDICTION: This change should improve overall image quality, especially texture and color details, but may also lead to increased training instability due to interplay between the two loss terms, and experimentation with the balance between the two losses will be necessary.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revised Feedback Loop Architecture
PROPOSAL: Revise the feedback loop architecture in 'Few-Step Generative Model with Improved Stability' to use a residual block structure, allowing the network to focus on refining the output from the previous step rather than starting anew. This is achieved by feeding the input of each step as a residual connection to the output of the previous step, thus creating a recursive structure that leverages the output from previous steps to improve the final result.
CONTROLS: Original PCM with static schedule, modified PCM with residual block structure
COST: No additional compute is needed, as the implementation can reuse existing resources, adding trivial marginal GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By using residual connections, the network is less prone to degradation paths and improved stability is expected, especially at low NFEs, but care must be taken in tuning the hyperparameters to avoid overfitting in the modified model.

PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to utilize a generative adversarial network (GAN) for learning a patch-based probability distribution from noisy point cloud samples. The generator will learn to produce a probabilistic distribution that captures the noise patterns in the point cloud, while the discriminator will differentiate between the original clean point cloud and the denoised output from the generator. This competitive process allows for a better estimation of the noise distribution and improves the overall denoising performance.
CONTROLS: Compare our revised approach against a baseline GAN architecture without patch-based probability distribution learning, and against the patch-based approach without the discriminator.
COST: 16 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our results indicate a significant improvement in denoising performance, with a reduction in mean squared error (MSE) and a better visual quality of the denoised output.

TITLE: masked autoencoder for point cloud denoising with reconstruction loss minimization
PROPOSAL: We propose a masked autoencoder model that incorporates a denoising autoencoder with a probabilistic reconstruction loss term to learn a mapping between the noisy point cloud and a clean representation. TITLE: consistency-based multi-agent reinforcement learning for unsupervised point cloud denoising
PROPOSAL: We propose a consistency-based multi-agent reinforcement learning approach for unsupervised point cloud denoising, where multiple agents collaborate to remove noise from the point cloud while maintaining consistency among their outputs. Each agent is trained to optimize a denoising objective function, and the multi-agent framework ensures that the agents learn to work together to achieve a common goal of removing noise while preserving the underlying structure of the point cloud.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach against existing reinforcement learning-based denoising methods and against a baseline multi-agent framework without consistency-based loss.

PREDICTION: Our results indicate a significant improvement in denoising performance and a better preservation of surface details, with a competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

TITLE: Unsupervised Denoising with Spatial Consistency Regularization
PROPOSAL: Adopt a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture with a novel loss function combining a spatial consistency term, encouraging denoised point clouds from different noisy observations to agree on their local geometry, and an adversarial term, incentivizing accuracy and fidelity in the denoised point cloud. * Additional control: It also includes a baseline for the impact that spatial consistency has on the optimization.

Potentially, only high-quality noise will be able to fool the model. The adversarial term encourages the model to learn the intra-point distances of clean point clouds thus significantly closing the gap with supervised denoising methods. ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Learning Failure Set via Weak Supervision for Reward Hacking Prevention
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new component to the policy optimization framework that learns a "failure set" of state-action pairs where the proxy reward diverges significantly from the true reward. This failure set is discovered through weak supervision from a surrogate loss, such as the KL-divergence between the learned policy's and the reference policy's state-action occupancy measures. The policy optimization objective is augmented with an additional regularization term that penalizes the learned policy's performance on the failure set.

ACTION: ADD 3

PROPOSAL: Modify the policy optimization objective to decouple the learned policy's performance into two components: one aligned with the proxy reward, and the other aligned with a informative prior model or knowledge graph that captures the structural relationships between the state and actions. ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Robust Reward Shaping through Consensus Optimization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a consensus optimization framework that ensembles multiple proxy rewards learned from partial and noisy observations, and regularizes their disagreement through a divergence-based objective. CONTROLS: Standard ORPO with and without the consensus optimization framework, and a baseline that uses a single proxy reward.

TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Derive general insights into the structure of zero-variance prompts and their implications for policy optimization. We will perform a theoretical analysis of the ratio of identical rewards to the standard deviations of the rewards, assuming that the LLM's responses can be modeled as a Gaussian process. This will allow us to identify the conditions under which zero-variance prompts are more likely to occur and to derive predictions for the optimal policies under these conditions. We will furthermore examine the effects of group relative policy optimization on the policy space and show how learned rewards from zero-variance prompts can be incorporated into the optimization process.
CONTROLS: Theoretical comparison with standard GRPO training.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (theoretical analysis).
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis will reveal that zero-variance prompts can be avoided if the ratio of identical rewards to the standard deviations is sufficiently large, and that learned rewards from these prompts can significantly improve performance by helping the model generalize to new scenarios; however, the results may be sensitive to the assumptions about the LLM's responses and the specific parametrization of the policy and reward functions.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Multiverse Policy Learning with Robust Chi-Squared Regularization
PROPOSAL: We learn a set of policies across a range of possible proxy rewards that are consistent with the assumed correlation constraint. Classically, policy optimization involves a trade-off between reward maximization and regularization. Here, we trade off across a distribution of proxies; our learning objective promotes policies that generalize across proxy rewards by pushing the chi-squared divergence with the reference policy's occupancy measure to be small on average across the set of proxies. The set of proxies is drawn according to its prior and the properties of the true reward; using prior knowledge about the reward structure, we encourage the learning algorithm to stay within the optimal risk set by choosing proxies for which the correlation constraint is guaranteed to hold.
CONTROLS: (1) classical policy-optimization baselines, (2) standard Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) as a proxy-targeting regularizer
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see robust improvements in true reward and, critically, worst-case risk guarantees against poorly specified proxy rewards, though the methods may be conservatively biased and potentially overly complex for problem-sizes smaller than the experiment.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Learning Failure Set via Weak Supervision for Reward Hacking Avoidance
PROPOSAL: When training under a single proxy reward, we observe that exploration occurs mainly in those regions of the state-action space that are poorly constrained by the reward and reference policy. Inspired by techniques for weak supervision of anomaly detection, we introduce weak labels that identify regions that the reference policy rarely or never visits. During policy optimization, these regions are penalized, encouraging the agent to visit them less aggressively. Our main claim is that the agent subsequently develops knowledge of the failure set - i.e., a low-cost subset of states that, when reached, typically lead to suboptimal behavior - thereby avoiding catastrophic failures in such regions and reducing the need for the proxy-reward correlation constraint.

TITLE: Multi-Antenna Deep Ranging with Adaptive Beamforming for Improved Signal-to-Noise Ratio
PROPOSAL: We design and evaluate a novel, multi-antenna RF sensing system that integrates deep learning-based beamforming to adaptively focus on the target object, reject noise, and improve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the input signal. This is achieved through a two-stage approach: first, a neural network processes the raw RF signal to predict 3D point cloud locations; second, an additional network adjusts beamforming weights to enhance the signal at these predicted locations. We train on a combination of datasets collected from real-world RF sensors and simulated scenarios, using metrics such as mean average precision (mAP) and mean square error (MSE) to evaluate performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against standard signal processing techniques (e.g., DAS beamforming) and a baseline-depth-only neural ranging approach, trained on the same datasets.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect an improvement of up to 30% in mAP and a 25% reduction in MSE compared to the baseline, especially in cluttered environments. The method may struggle in low-SNR scenarios and might require extensive tuning.

TITLE: Random Field Regularization for Millimeter-Wave RF Signal Denoising
PROPOSAL: To address the high noise levels in mmWave RF signals, we propose a novel approach that incorporates random field regularization into a denoising neural network. This is inspired by the fact that RF signals follow a Gaussian process in space and time. By incorporating this prior information into the network's loss function, we encourage the network to produce smooth and coherent reconstructions, even in the presence of corrupting noise. We train the network on a variety of datasets containing MMwave RF signals and evaluate its performance using metrics such as the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR).
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against standard denoising techniques (e.g., median filtering, total variation regularization) and a baseline neural network trained without regularization.
COST: 550 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a 15-20% improvement in SNR and a 12-15% improvement in PSNR compared to the baseline, especially in highly noisy environments. However, the method may struggle in scenarios where signal artifacts are present, such as through-occlusion cases.

PROPOSAL: Utilize the Motion Coherence Theory to analyze the directional distributions of motion in each video sequence. PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate novel, computationally-efficient architectural variants of existing temporal change description methods (e.g., Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), or Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (TGCNs)) adapted for long-range temporal dynamics, using real-world satellite imagery benchmarks (e.g., Sentinel-2 time series) and metrics like mean average precision (mAP) and precision at 1, 5, and 10 (P@1, P@5, P@10).

TITLE: Diversity-Aware Interaction Representation for Robust Neuron Classification
PROPOSAL: We extend the Interaction-REP model (from proposal 1) by incorporating a diversity-aware component that aims to capture and leverage diversity in neural subpopulations. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Learning of Neuron-Specific Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical learning approach to extract neuron-specific representations from population activity. In the first stage, a autoencoder is trained to learn a compact representation of population activity, focusing on common features across neurons. In the second stage, a predictor network is trained on top of the autoencoder to learn neuron-specific representations by leveraging the diversity in population activity. This approach allows the model to capture both shared and unique aspects of neural activity, enabling robust neuron classification and brain region identification. We will evaluate this approach on Neuropixels recordings and calcium imaging data, focusing on tasks such as cell type classification and brain region identification.
CONTROLS: (1) Random forest baseline, (2) Interaction-REP, (3) Ablation of the second predictor network.
COST: 200000
PREDICTION: We expect to outperform the baseline and Interaction-REP on neuron classification tasks, especially in high-dimensional data settings. However, the hierarchical approach may suffer from increased computational cost and potential overfitting issues.
